PAPER: Journal of Dharma Studies (2026) 9:3 https://doi.org/10.1007/s42240-025-00234-y ORIGINAL ARTICLE A Hermeneutical Study of “Śamatha and Vipaśyanā Focused on the Combined Teachings” in the Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra Bin Liu1 Received: 4 November 2024 / Accepted: 4 November 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract This article is an attempt to address the gap in contemporary scholarship related to a unique form of śamatha and vipaśyanā, which focuses on the combined teach- ings, contributing to the research on the relationship between religious practice and religious philosophy, particularly regarding Mahāyāna Buddhism. Based on textual study and philosophical analysis of ancient Buddhist literatures, this article states that within the text of the Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra, “śamatha and vipaśyanā focused on the combined teachings” is effective and feasible in realizing the ulti- mate reality. This article concludes that the essential practice involves combining all the teachings and meditating on their collective contribution to the realization of suchness. The relationship between it and the theory of suchness is delineated into three aspects. First, meditating on the reasons that all the teachings contribute to the realization is itself a practice of suchness. Second, the entirety of all the teachings corresponds to the universality of suchness. Third, it is also a method to practice the suchness of the teachings themselves. Lastly, through the initial application of attention, sustained attention, and resolution, it is feasible for ordinary persons to engage in this practice and eventually realize suchness. Śamatha usually involves focusing on an object, such as breathing or compassion, together with the removal of various mental distractions, thereby cultivating a whole- some state of concentration. Building on this foundation, vipaśyanā refers to analyz- ing and observing its object in accordance with perspectives derived from Buddhist teachings, such as meditation on the impermanence of the body, thereby fostering the ability to perceive the reality as it is. However, contemporary academic research on the Yogācāra philosophy has not paid sufficient attention to the theories of śamatha and vipaśyanā, particularly when compared to the focus on the three-nature theory, consciousness-only theory, epis- temology, as well as their relationship to emptiness and Buddha-nature. One reason for this phenomenon may be that those latter theories are so distinctive that they are often regarded as the defining theories of Yogācāra,2 whereas śamatha and vipaśyanā are fundamental meditation methods in Buddhist practice and are found in other Bud- dhist schools as well. This article argues that although the basic concepts and meth- ods of śamatha and vipaśyanā are universal among various Buddhist schools, certain śamatha and vipaśyanā theories with distinctive ideological interpretations still exist in Yogācāra. Schmithausen (2007, 225) also points out that a Buddhist school’s the- ory of practice inherently mirrors its own philosophical framework. The “Maitreya Chapter” of this sutra, devoted specifically to śamatha and vipaśyanā, can serve as a basis for further research on the Yogācāra theory of these practices. Despite its uniqueness, the śamatha and vipaśyanā that focus on the “combined teachings” (Tib. ’dres pa’i chos; Ch. zong fa 總法) within the “Maitreya Chapter” has received little scholarly attention. Jōshō Nozawa (1957) offers a translation of Jñānagarbha’s and Byang chub rdzu ’phrul’s commentaries on this chapter along with his comments. Although he (1957, 243) suggests that “focused on the combined teachings” is equivalent to saṃbhinna-ālambanaḥ in the MSA, the mechanisms and reasoning underlying this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā are not elaborated in detail. Liu (2010, 84–5) states that this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā embodies the prac- tice of wisdom to distinguish specific phenomena as part of the Mahāyāna wisdom, which provides an important philosophical perspective for evaluating this medita- tion method. Further exploration would help clarify the relationship between this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā and suchness (Skt. tathatā; Tib. de bzhin nyid; Ch. zhenru 真如). Lin (2021, 52–3) proposes that the soteriological philosophy of this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā is rooted in the distinction between ineffable nature and designated nature of phenomena. In addition, the distinction between phenom- ena and teachings as objects of meditation could be further developed. Brunnhölzl (2018, 561) quotes the relevant text in the SNS to annotate “dharmas in fusion” in Asvabhāva’s Mahāyānasaṃgrahopanibandhana (MSU), suggesting his standpoint that the SNS and the MSU are addressing the same issue. Lin (2021, 248) also asserts that the MSU provides elaboration on the specific method for this meditation. An analysis of the terminological differences between the two treatises could further enhance this line of research. Although not focused on this issue, modern translations nonetheless reflect the translators’ interpretive choices. For instance, the recent translation by the Bud- dhavacana Translation Group (BTG) (2024, 78) renders it as “the mental stillness and insight with a universal teaching as a referential object.” Readers may find that this wording foregrounds the aspect of universality while making less explicit the com- bination of the teachings into a whole, as emphasized in both Chinese and Tibetan translations. Additionally, when translating the relationship between the combined teachings and suchness, Powers (1995, 163) employs the phrase “flow into suchness, descend into suchness, have descended into suchness.” The distinction between the terms “flow” and “descend” could be more clearly articulated. In conclusion, several issues concerning “śamatha and vipaśyanā focused on the combined teachings” remain open for further study. First, the literal meanings of this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā merit detailed examination. This necessitates a thorough analysis of the relevant passages in the Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra and its com- mentaries, with particular emphasis on the key term “combined teachings.” Second, the effectiveness of this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā in attaining enlightenment deserves further investigation. This issue involves the soteriological philosophy of this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā and requires exploration of its relationship to the ultimate reality presented in the SNS. Third, the feasibility of practicing this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā from a mental perspective requires examination. This inquiry is crucial because it pertains to the practical application of this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā, particularly for an ordinary person (Skt. pṛthagjana; Tib. so so skye 1 3 Journal of Dharma Studies (2026) 9:3 Page 5 of 35 3 bo; Ch. fanfu 凡夫). However, it remains unexplored in contemporary scholarship. Consequently, this article seeks to advance research on the “śamatha and vipaśyanā focused on the combined teachings” through these three dimensions. The methodology employed in this article is the philosophical and textual study of both Chinese and Tibetan translations of the SNS, supplemented by an examination of several ancient commentaries. Modern scholarship is also consulted and analyzed. This article proposes that within the text of the Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra, the practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā focused on the combined teachings is effective and fea- sible in realizing the ultimate reality. The Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra and the “Maitreya Chapter” Sources and Translated Versions To date, no complete manuscripts of the Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra (SNS)4 have been discovered. Although some Sanskrit fragments exist and modern scholarship has published portions quoted in other Sanskrit treatises, none of these cover the target texts related to this article.5 Therefore, this research is based on the ancient Chinese and Tibetan translations. There are four ancient Chinese translations of this sutra. Two of them are par- tial translations by Guṇabhadra (5th century CE) and Paramārtha (6th century CE), neither of which covers the “Maitreya Chapter.” During the 6th century, Bodhiruci translated the entire sutra as Shenmi Jietuo Jing (深密解脫經; Profound Mystery and Liberation; T. 16, no. 675). The latest complete translation, Jie Shenmi Jing (解深密 經; Unravelling the Profound Mystery; T. 16, no. 676), is attributed to Xuanzang in the 7th century and is the most popular version in East Asian Buddhism. For the Tibetan translation, based on the Kanjur, Étienne-Louis Lamotte offered a modern critical edition titled Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra L’explication des Mystères: Texte Tibétain in 1935, which is the most widely consulted among contemporary scholars.6 However, Lamotte’s transliteration does not fully align with the now widely used Wylie system; for convenience, the paragraphs cited from his edition in this article are converted into Wylie. Following Lamotte, Hakamaya (1984, 192) published his findings on an older Tibetan translation of this sutra preserved in Dun- huang, stating that this version was translated before the establishment of “the finally decided [translation] words [system]” (Tib. skad gsar bcad). Additionally, there are four relatively well-known contemporary English transla- tions of the SNS. John Powers translated it from Tibetan into English and published it in 1995. However, why are the Buddha’s teachings one of the neces- sary bases and abodes for a bodhisattva to practice śamatha and vipaśyanā? In his commentary, Woncheuk explains that without hearing from the Buddha, one cannot realize the ineffable nature (Skt. nirabhilāpyasvabhāva; Tib. brjod du med pa’i ngo bo nyid; Ch. liyan zixing 離言自性) of all phenomena.9 As stated in the YBh, the ineffable nature of all phenomena should be known inasmuch as the inherent nature of phenomena does not exist as it is expressed, but it is not true that nothing exists in any way.10 Woncheuk’s interpretation suggests that for an ordinary person who clings to the nature of phenomena as expressed, the ineffable nature is beyond the scope of thought and cognition without external intervention. Consequently, the ordinary person will remain in the vortex of constant attachment and be unable to transcend it. In the “Maitreya Chapter” of the SNS, the practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā begins with receiving and contemplating the Buddha’s teachings, which are classified into twelve branches (Skt. dvādaśāṅga[pravacana]; Tib. gsung rab yan lag bcu gnyis; Ch. shi’erfen jiao 十 二分教). Key Terms: Zongfa and ’dres Pa’i Chos Xuanzang’s translation names this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā as yuan zongfa shemota piboshena 緣總法奢摩他毘鉢舍那, while the Tibetan translation refers to it as ’dres pa’i chos la dmigs pa’i zhi gnas dang lhag mthong. Most parts of these two expressions are straightforward, except for zongfa 總法 and ’dres pa’i chos, which are the key terms in this phrase. It is well-known that fa and chos are both translated from the Sanskrit term dharma. However, in Buddhism, dharma occurs frequently and conveys different meanings in various context. In his Vyākhyāyukti, Vasubandhu summarizes ten meanings of dharma (Mathes, 2008, p. 193): “Knowable objects, the path, nirvāṇa, the objects of the mental faculty, merit, life, the discourses [of the Buddha], [entities] consisting of elements, certainty and law.” Additionally, dharma is qualified by zong and ’dres pa, making it difficult to infer the meaning of these key terms literally. In the context of the SNS, zongfa 總法 and ’dres pa’i chos should be understood as “combined teachings.” This is because, when referring to this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā, it is explicitly stated that the Buddha’s teachings, such as the sutra collec- tion, are gathered into one, united into one, summarized into one, and they form one aggregate.14 Therefore, dharma here simply refers to the Buddha’s teachings rather than other meanings; hence, I employ “teachings” to translate this term. According to the sutra’s description, the qualifier of “teachings” expresses the meanings of “merging,” “gathering,” “combining,” and “mixing” the Buddha’s teachings. Thus, śamatha and vipaśyanā focused on the combined teachings will take all the teachings as the object, and through this practice, the various virtues within these teachings will be developed by the practitioner. Conclusions This article examines the śamatha and vipaśyanā focused on the combined teachings in the “Maitreya Chapter” of the Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra. Among a few scholars who have addressed this topic, three main questions still invite further discussion. First, the literal meanings of this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā in both Chinese and Tibetan translations. Second, the soteriological philosophy of this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā, specifically why it is effective in realizing the truth. Third, the feasibility of this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā, especially for mundane persons. First, this article analyzes the literal meanings of this phrase, investigates the cor- responding Chinese, Tibetan translations and possible Sanskrit terminologies of the key terms, and ultimately delineates a four-step method for its practice. Subsequently, it summarizes the three subtypes mentioned in the sutra, highlighting that the primary differences among them pertain to the scope of the meditative object. Next, this article delves into the soteriological philosophy of this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā to examine its effectiveness. It concludes that meditating that why all the teachings are helpful in realizing suchness either directly or indirectly is itself a practice of suchness. Second, the wholeness of all the teachings corresponds to the universality of suchness. Third, it is also a manner to practice the suchness of the teachings themselves. Regarding the feasibility of this form of śamatha and vipaśyanā, it primarily dis- cusses three mental factors: initial application of attention, sustained attention, and resolution. JSON: Name: sns_combined_teachings_pipeline Title: An integrated philological and empirical pipeline combining critical-text collation and randomized interventions to evaluate the efficacy and feasibility of Saṃdhinirmocana-derived śamatha–vipaśyanā focused on the combined teachings Short Hypothesis: Meditation instruction protocols derived from the Saṃdhinirmocana sutra’s combined-teachings formulation cause greater increases in (a) conceptual integration (measured by a standardized conceptual-flexibility task) and (b) resolution-related phenomenology (measured by a resolution scale and coded phenomenological interviews), than single-teaching-focused protocols after an 8-week training period. Related Work: Prior scholarship has produced (1) critical and vernacular translations of the Saṃdhinirmocana and its Maitreya chapter with divergent renderings of the key phrase variously translated as combined/mixed/integrated teachings; (2) doctrinal and hermeneutical analyses framing śamatha and vipaśyanā within Yogācāra epistemology and three-nature theory; and (3) comparative work on śamatha/vipaśyanā categories in Yogācāra treatises such as the Yogācārabhūmi and Mahāyānasaṃgraha. Existing work is limited by (a) inconsistent handling of Chinese and Tibetan witness texts and uncertainty about the underlying Sanskrit term; (b) lack of systematic collation across commentarial traditions to resolve semantic range of the term ‘combined teachings’; and (c) absence of controlled empirical tests linking distinct textual meditative prescriptions to measurable cognitive or phenomenological outcomes. No prior study jointly operationalizes philological disambiguation with experimental testing of meditation instruction variants. Abstract: This project builds a structured research pipeline that integrates critical philology, hermeneutical analysis, and empirical testing to evaluate the Saṃdhinirmocana sutra’s śamatha–vipaśyanā “focused on the combined teachings.” First, the pipeline will produce a synchronized digital collation of Chinese and Tibetan witnesses and extant Sanskrit fragments together with major ancient commentaries to disambiguate the operative terminology and reconstruct stepwise practice instructions. Second, those hermeneutically derived instructions will be operationalized into reproducible meditation protocols: (A) combined-teachings protocol (all teachings aggregated and contemplated), (B) single-teaching protocol (individual teaching-focused), and (C) active control (standard attention training). Third, the pipeline will test the causal effect of protocol type in a randomized, pre-registered 8-week intervention measuring conceptual integration, resolution-related phenomenology, sustained attention, and physiological markers. The expected contribution is twofold: a transparent text-critical foundation for interpreting the Maitreya chapter and empirical evidence whether the combined-teachings format produces distinct cognitive and phenomenological outcomes compared to single-teaching instruction. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Textual corpus: Xuanzang T.16 recension, Bodhiruci recension, Lamotte Tibetan critical edition (Wylie), Phug-brag and Derge Kanjur witnesses, extant Sanskrit fragments, commentaries by Asaṅga, Jñānagarbha, Woncheuk, Byang chub rdzu 'phrul, Asvabhāva, and Paramārtha; (2) Participant dataset: two cohorts: novice meditators (n=90) and experienced practitioners (n=90), total n=180. Baselines: (i) single-teaching protocol (operationalized from Maitreya chapter focusing on a single sutra teaching), (ii) active attention-control protocol (mindfulness-based attention training), (iii) combined-teachings protocol (operationalized from collated text). Randomization: stratified by cohort and prior meditation hours into three arms per cohort (n=30 per arm). Intervention: 8 weeks, 3 sessions/week, 45 minutes/session, standardized audio-guided instructions. Primary outcome measures: (A) conceptual integration score from a validated conceptual-flexibility battery (pre/post), (B) resolution scale (new or adapted psychometric instrument; pre/post); Secondary measures: nondual awareness questionnaire, Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) reaction time and error rates, EEG frontal midline theta power, heart rate variability (HRV). Textual-analysis metrics: token-level alignment divergence, translation-variant frequency, inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa) on hermeneutic annotations. Ablation studies: (1) combined protocol minus step 2 (no aggregation), (2) combined protocol minus step 3 (no contemplation of suchness), (3) combined protocol with only one tense framing (e.g., only 'will fall into'). Statistical analysis: mixed-effects ANOVA for pre/post and between-arm comparisons, planned contrasts between combined vs single and combined vs control, correction for multiple comparisons (Benjamini-Hochberg), effect size estimation (Cohen's d), mediation analysis to test if resolution mediates the protocol->integration effect. Power calculation: detect d=0.6 with 80% power at alpha=0.05 requires n≈30 per arm. Pre-registration and data/code release required. Risk Factors and Limitations: Textual risks: absence of a complete Sanskrit witness creates irreducible uncertainty in semantic reconstruction; collational alignment noise may bias operationalization. Operationalization risks: translating layered hermeneutic practice steps into short, standardized audio protocols may omit pragmatic elements critical in traditional pedagogy. Measurement risks: psychometric instruments for 'resolution' or 'suchness-related phenomenology' may lack established validity; developing and validating a new scale will add noise and delay. Participant risks: recruitment bias toward Westernized or secular meditators may limit generalizability to traditional practitioners; adherence variability and expectancy/placebo effects may confound outcomes. Technical risks: EEG/HRV signals may be noisy in field settings; small sample sizes for neurophysiological measures may underpower detection. Analytical risks: multiple comparisons and heterogeneity between novice and experienced cohorts may complicate inference. Ethical/cultural limits: imposing textually derived practices outside their cultural-religious context risks misinterpretation and may limit acceptance by source communities. Scalability: the pipeline depends on interdisciplinary expertise (philology, contemplative pedagogy, cognitive neuroscience), constraining replication without comparable resources.
